the self-assembling peptides are able to catalyze the hydrolysis of esters in aqueous solution, that the catalytic activity of the peptides is enhanced by the presence of the self-assembled nanoparticles, and that the nanoparticles can be used as a template for the immobilization of the peptides on a solid support.

peptide-based nanoparticles can be designed that accelerate esterase-catalyzed ester hydrolyses, and that the catalytic efficiency can be tuned by variation of the peptide sequence and the surface charge of the nanoparticles.
peptide-based catalysts are capable of accelerating chemical reactions, and that the activity of the catalyst is enhanced by self-assembly.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the design of biomimetic catalysts for the hydrolysis of esters and the elucidation of structure-activity relationships.
the synthesis, characterization, and application of peptide-based materials.
the development of new concepts for the design and preparation of functional peptide-based materials, with a particular focus on the self-assembly of peptides into well-defined nanostructures.

the peptide-based catalysts are not enzymes.
the peptide nanoparticles are an excellent model for the enzyme catalyzed reaction.
the catalytic activity of these peptide nanoparticles is not due to any single factor, but is a result of the synergistic interplay of the different factors.
